compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In a fictional project, both colleagues receive the same delay notice and can review the same alternatives. Either may contact the client or check staffing. What they do depends partly on their responsibilities and what the project needs.

The shared E concerns outward attention and energy. The shared N concerns giving weight to patterns and possibilities. The letters do not tell you which colleague will take the lead or how quickly the team will reach a decision.

The difference sits in the other two. T/F changes the basis: the ENTJ side more often asks which route loses less under the same constraints and whether that standard can be applied to every module; the ENFP side more often asks what this choice means for the client, the team and the person concerned, and whose situation has been left out. J/P changes how the close works: the ENTJ side more often closes dates, owners and the outward line into one version; the ENFP side more often keeps one more route open before settling, waiting for new information.

Both bases and both closings are available to both. When the client writes that any change of date means a claim, someone leaning ENFP may also converge quickly and drive execution; when the plan is clearly unworkable and the team has been working late for weeks, someone leaning ENTJ may also demand a different route.

### ENFP and ENTJ: the same delay notice, two kinds of basis

In a fictional project review, both colleagues receive the same delay notice, staffing information, sign-off requirements and supplier options. The opening date is unchanged.

For T/F, either colleague can assess the impact on the people preparing the launch or apply the same staffing, scope and deadline criteria to each option. For J/P, either can agree on a provisional plan or keep several workable options open while waiting for the same reply.

These are separate questions: what makes one option preferable, and when to commit to it. Either person can use both kinds of criteria and either approach to planning.

Each approach has a cost. Spread too wide, the team keeps changing direction and is back where it started two days later; close too fast, and what gets cut may be exactly what the client cares about most. The size of the cost has nothing to do with preference; it depends on who holds the supplier information, who has decision authority, and who signs for delivery.

The test has to leave room. Change the conditions and either may switch; a single choice describes this occasion's information and duty, and cannot be used to classify.

### ENFP and ENTJ: why Fi and Te are shared while both perceiving functions change

In the four-function notation used here, ENFP is Ne–Fi–Te–Si and ENTJ is Te–Ni–Se–Fi. What is shared is the two judging processes: Te third in ENFP and first in ENTJ, Fi second in ENFP and fourth in ENTJ. What changes is the perceiving pair: Ne to Ni, Si to Se.

The reason is that two letters change at once. J/P changes the category of the extraverted dominant process: both are E types in this model, and ENTJ's extraverted dominant is the judging process Te while ENFP's is the perceiving process Ne. That is a label of a theoretical category, not the order of real steps, and it does not mean that the one who judges first is more decisive. T/F changes the rank of the judging processes: both use standards and values, and what differs is which side gets leaned on first — Te ahead on the ENTJ side, Fi ahead on the ENFP side.

Both stacks include Fi and Te, but at different positions. The order describes the model and cannot establish who will make a better plan or work more effectively with clients.

Whether the third position (Te in ENFP, Se in ENTJ) is marked introverted or extraverted is not uniform across tables. This page takes the common version and treats it as a secondary clue only, not for inferring behaviour order or areas of strength. Base descriptions sit on the [ENFP profile](/en/personality/enfp) and the [ENTJ profile](/en/personality/entj).

compare_blocks.body:
Boundary of use: the three scenes below are editorial demonstrations, used only to see how the same information gets read with different emphasis. They are not for typing and not for allocating posts. Whether a pairing works depends far more on who holds the supplier information, who has decision authority and who signs for the client.

### ENFP and ENTJ: covering a two-week delay the client will not accept

(Fictional scene) A store system was due to launch at month end; a third-party payment interface slipped and the whole thing moves to the middle of next month. The client replies with one line: the opening date cannot move, find a way.

One may go and ask first: can the payment provider open a sandbox, can another provider cover the interim, can the client open with checkout but without the membership feature. What is attended to is which routes remain and what each means for the opening. The other may lay the three routes out by cost first: switching provider means rebuilding the reconciliation, opening a sandbox needs the client to configure testing, cutting membership needs sales to agree; then fix one main route and one fallback, and write into the group when the decision must be made. Who takes which segment usually depends on who knows the provider and who can amend the contract, not on type.

The costs differ: too many routes and the team keeps turning, back at the start two days later; too fast a close and the part cut is the part the client cared about. A workable pairing agrees the exploration deadline and the give-ups in advance, with the deadline set by project complexity and contract milestones rather than a generic number of hours.

The evidence that counts is whether the plan states what is being given up. A plan listing only new actions and no give-ups usually breaks in the second week of execution. Counterexamples: with the client writing that any change of date means a claim, someone leaning ENFP may also converge immediately; when the team cannot sustain it, someone leaning ENTJ may also go to the client to renegotiate scope.

A check: write two versions of the recovery plan — one adjusting scope (what gets delivered less), one adjusting staffing (who joins, for how many days) — and mark in each the item that breaks first. If both point at the same place, check the shared bottleneck first: the same interface, the same approval, the same group of people. If they point at different places, align each assumption, dependency and acceptable loss, then see whether there really is a difference in risk appetite. Writing fast or slow cannot be used to judge preference.

### ENFP and ENTJ: mid-project, the technical approach turns out not to work

(Fictional scene) Four months in, the synchronous design drops orders when a store's network is unstable, and switching to asynchronous means rewriting half of it.

One may look first for a third route: local caching only in weak-network stores, pushing the drop rate down to something acceptable, a partial rollout across a few stores first. The other may calculate the cost of switching against not switching: how many person-weeks to rewrite half, whether the delay collides with a contract milestone, and what the worst-case compensation is if it does not switch.

Both calculations may conclude switch or do not switch, and may land on the same route for different reasons. Whether it is reversible has to rest on conditions: a small-scale trial only makes sense when dropped orders can be fully detected, reliably re-entered, and the affected scope is contained; if drops cannot be reconciled, key data cannot be recovered, or re-entry conflicts with reconciliation, the trial should not be widened until the risk is cleared. These conditions apply to both people equally and do not change with type.

### ENFP and ENTJ: a partner wants a twenty-thousand diving course

(Fictional scene) The way trade-offs are made at work turns up in a shared household too, with more constraints: budget, time, care arrangements, and what each person cares about.

In a fictional household decision, one partner wants to take a costly diving course that would occupy three weekends. Both can discuss what the experience would mean to the person taking the course and apply the same budget and scheduling criteria they use for similar commitments.

The household can consider personal value and practical constraints together. Either person can ask whether the budget can absorb the course, how responsibilities would be covered and why the course matters to their partner.

A check: each writes one line on when this money would count as well spent, then swaps and reads. If the two lines are far apart, align three things first: the budget ceiling, the care arrangement for those three weekends, and what each most wants out of it — the experience, the certificate, or doing it together. If both still want it after that, discuss whether to start with a trial session; instalments are a payment arrangement, not a conclusion, and whether it can be split depends on the provider and the household's cash flow.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
Reading ENFP as only producing ideas and never landing them is the most common misreading of this pair. In a recovery they often write the plan as a timetable too, only with more versions and faster revisions; more versions does not mean no landing, and fast revision does not mean no standard.

Reading ENTJ as indifferent to how the team feels is also wrong. Some ENTJs seek people out after the meeting, some do not; whether they care depends on the specific people and relationship, cannot be deduced from four letters, and cannot be deduced from one meeting where they did not respond.

The third misreads T/F as who is harder. In a recovery, hardness depends on the contract terms, the duty and the tolerable cost; the same person behaves completely differently in front of two contracts, one with a penalty clause and one without.

The fourth reads J/P as who is more urgent and who drags. J/P describes whether the outward stance leans closing or keeping open — not execution, and not reliability. Someone who closes fast may miss a condition; someone who keeps it open may be waiting for a reply that will never come.

(Fictional scene) A store system was due to launch at month end; a third-party payment interface slipped and the whole thing moves to the middle of next month. The client replies with one line: the opening date cannot move, find a way.

body: In a fictional project, both colleagues receive the same delay notice and can review the same alternatives. Either may contact the client or check staffing. What they do depends partly on their responsibilities and what the project needs.

The shared E concerns outward attention and energy. The shared N concerns giving weight to patterns and possibilities. The letters do not tell you which colleague will take the lead or how quickly the team will reach a decision.

The difference sits in the other two. T/F changes the basis: the ENTJ side more often asks which route loses less under the same constraints and whether that standard can be applied to every module; the ENFP side more often asks what this choice means for the client, the team and the person concerned, and whose situation has been left out. J/P changes how the close works: the ENTJ side more often closes dates, owners and the outward line into one version; the ENFP side more often keeps one more route open before settling, waiting for new information.

Both bases and both closings are available to both. When the client writes that any change of date means a claim, someone leaning ENFP may also converge quickly and drive execution; when the plan is clearly unworkable and the team has been working late for weeks, someone leaning ENTJ may also demand a different route.
### ENFP and ENTJ: the same delay notice, two kinds of basis
In a fictional project review, both colleagues receive the same delay notice, staffing information, sign-off requirements and supplier options. The opening date is unchanged.

For T/F, either colleague can assess the impact on the people preparing the launch or apply the same staffing, scope and deadline criteria to each option. For J/P, either can agree on a provisional plan or keep several workable options open while waiting for the same reply.
These are separate questions: what makes one option preferable, and when to commit to it. Either person can use both kinds of criteria and either approach to planning.

Each approach has a cost. Spread too wide, the team keeps changing direction and is back where it started two days later; close too fast, and what gets cut may be exactly what the client cares about most. The size of the cost has nothing to do with preference; it depends on who holds the supplier information, who has decision authority, and who signs for delivery.
The test has to leave room. Change the conditions and either may switch; a single choice describes this occasion's information and duty, and cannot be used to classify.
### ENFP and ENTJ: why Fi and Te are shared while both perceiving functions change

In the four-function notation used here, ENFP is Ne–Fi–Te–Si and ENTJ is Te–Ni–Se–Fi. What is shared is the two judging processes: Te third in ENFP and first in ENTJ, Fi second in ENFP and fourth in ENTJ. What changes is the perceiving pair: Ne to Ni, Si to Se.

The reason is that two letters change at once. J/P changes the category of the extraverted dominant process: both are E types in this model, and ENTJ's extraverted dominant is the judging process Te while ENFP's is the perceiving process Ne. That is a label of a theoretical category, not the order of real steps, and it does not mean that the one who judges first is more decisive. T/F changes the rank of the judging processes: both use standards and values, and what differs is which side gets leaned on first — Te ahead on the ENTJ side, Fi ahead on the ENFP side.
Both stacks include Fi and Te, but at different positions. The order describes the model and cannot establish who will make a better plan or work more effectively with clients.

Whether the third position (Te in ENFP, Se in ENTJ) is marked introverted or extraverted is not uniform across tables. This page takes the common version and treats it as a secondary clue only, not for inferring behaviour order or areas of strength. Base descriptions sit on the [ENFP profile](/en/personality/enfp) and the [ENTJ profile](/en/personality/entj).

body: Align the conditions first: the same number of delay days, the same people available, the same client, the same contract terms. If one is the project manager and the other only helping out, or the client has already written in a penalty, role and constraint will swamp both columns and the difference narrows.

Each row states which kind of evidence may be attended to first in the same scene, not a fixed action. Both types can take the other's approach; the table only describes what tends to be taken first, and the last column marks whether the row sits closer to T/F or J/P.

| The same scene (same delay, same people, same client) | ENFP: the kind of evidence likely to be taken first | ENTJ: the kind of evidence likely to be taken first | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What the first round of discussion adds | Weigh what the same delivery options mean for the people preparing the launch | Apply the same staffing, scope and deadline criteria to each delivery option | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F |
| Both assess the same options for three modules | Weigh how changes would affect customers and the teams that rely on each module | Apply the same capacity and acceptance criteria to every option | Decision criteria: T/F |
| How finished the plan is before it goes out | Keep several workable plans open while both wait for the same client feedback | Agree on a provisional plan and mark what may change after the same feedback | Outward stance, leaning J/P |
| Both decide what to prioritize in the same client update | Weigh what the change means for the people preparing to open the store | Apply the same criteria for relevance and accuracy used in comparable updates | Decision criteria: T/F |
| Both have the same assignments and staffing information still pending | Keep two workable staffing plans available until the same availability information is confirmed | Agree on a provisional staffing plan and set a time to review it | Approach to outward arrangements: J/P |
| Both plan a follow-up to the same review | Keep two feasible changes open until the team has the same feedback | Agree on one provisional change and set a time to revisit it | Approach to outward arrangements: J/P |

None of these rows is a scale of ability. An ENFP with years in delivery may open the staffing sheet first; an ENTJ just handed the project may ask everywhere for alternatives. body: Boundary of use: the three scenes below are editorial demonstrations, used only to see how the same information gets read with different emphasis. They are not for typing and not for allocating posts. Whether a pairing works depends far more on who holds the supplier information, who has decision authority and who signs for the client.
### ENFP and ENTJ: covering a two-week delay the client will not accept

(Fictional scene) A store system was due to launch at month end; a third-party payment interface slipped and the whole thing moves to the middle of next month. The client replies with one line: the opening date cannot move, find a way.

One may go and ask first: can the payment provider open a sandbox, can another provider cover the interim, can the client open with checkout but without the membership feature. What is attended to is which routes remain and what each means for the opening. The other may lay the three routes out by cost first: switching provider means rebuilding the reconciliation, opening a sandbox needs the client to configure testing, cutting membership needs sales to agree; then fix one main route and one fallback, and write into the group when the decision must be made. Who takes which segment usually depends on who knows the provider and who can amend the contract, not on type.

The costs differ: too many routes and the team keeps turning, back at the start two days later; too fast a close and the part cut is the part the client cared about. A workable pairing agrees the exploration deadline and the give-ups in advance, with the deadline set by project complexity and contract milestones rather than a generic number of hours.

The evidence that counts is whether the plan states what is being given up. A plan listing only new actions and no give-ups usually breaks in the second week of execution. Counterexamples: with the client writing that any change of date means a claim, someone leaning ENFP may also converge immediately; when the team cannot sustain it, someone leaning ENTJ may also go to the client to renegotiate scope.

A check: write two versions of the recovery plan — one adjusting scope (what gets delivered less), one adjusting staffing (who joins, for how many days) — and mark in each the item that breaks first. If both point at the same place, check the shared bottleneck first: the same interface, the same approval, the same group of people. If they point at different places, align each assumption, dependency and acceptable loss, then see whether there really is a difference in risk appetite. Writing fast or slow cannot be used to judge preference.
### ENFP and ENTJ: mid-project, the technical approach turns out not to work
(Fictional scene) Four months in, the synchronous design drops orders when a store's network is unstable, and switching to asynchronous means rewriting half of it.

One may look first for a third route: local caching only in weak-network stores, pushing the drop rate down to something acceptable, a partial rollout across a few stores first. The other may calculate the cost of switching against not switching: how many person-weeks to rewrite half, whether the delay collides with a contract milestone, and what the worst-case compensation is if it does not switch.

Both calculations may conclude switch or do not switch, and may land on the same route for different reasons. Whether it is reversible has to rest on conditions: a small-scale trial only makes sense when dropped orders can be fully detected, reliably re-entered, and the affected scope is contained; if drops cannot be reconciled, key data cannot be recovered, or re-entry conflicts with reconciliation, the trial should not be widened until the risk is cleared. These conditions apply to both people equally and do not change with type.
### ENFP and ENTJ: a partner wants a twenty-thousand diving course
(Fictional scene) The way trade-offs are made at work turns up in a shared household too, with more constraints: budget, time, care arrangements, and what each person cares about.

In a fictional household decision, one partner wants to take a costly diving course that would occupy three weekends. Both can discuss what the experience would mean to the person taking the course and apply the same budget and scheduling criteria they use for similar commitments.

The household can consider personal value and practical constraints together. Either person can ask whether the budget can absorb the course, how responsibilities would be covered and why the course matters to their partner.

A check: each writes one line on when this money would count as well spent, then swaps and reads. If the two lines are far apart, align three things first: the budget ceiling, the care arrangement for those three weekends, and what each most wants out of it — the experience, the certificate, or doing it together. If both still want it after that, discuss whether to start with a trial session; instalments are a payment arrangement, not a conclusion, and whether it can be split depends on the provider and the household's cash flow.

body: Reading ENFP as only producing ideas and never landing them is the most common misreading of this pair. In a recovery they often write the plan as a timetable too, only with more versions and faster revisions; more versions does not mean no landing, and fast revision does not mean no standard.

Reading ENTJ as indifferent to how the team feels is also wrong. Some ENTJs seek people out after the meeting, some do not; whether they care depends on the specific people and relationship, cannot be deduced from four letters, and cannot be deduced from one meeting where they did not respond.

The third misreads T/F as who is harder. In a recovery, hardness depends on the contract terms, the duty and the tolerable cost; the same person behaves completely differently in front of two contracts, one with a penalty clause and one without.

The fourth reads J/P as who is more urgent and who drags. J/P describes whether the outward stance leans closing or keeping open — not execution, and not reliability. Someone who closes fast may miss a condition; someone who keeps it open may be waiting for a reply that will never come.

body: When two results differ, check the item bank, language version and scoring definition first, then the circumstances: were you signing for the outcome, did you have enough information, how tight was the deadline. ENFP and ENTJ share Extraversion (E) and Intuition (N). They differ in the criteria they tend to weigh in decisions (T/F) and how they tend to approach outward arrangements (J/P).

- E (Extraversion): attention and energy turn more often toward the project, the client and the people present. It describes direction, not social skill, and does not guarantee being the first to step forward when something breaks.
- N (Intuition): information lands first on connections, patterns and possibility rather than on facts checked one by one. Both share this side, so both easily open with how else this could go.
- T/F: the ENTJ side's T more often weighs by impersonal criteria that apply consistently; the ENFP side's F more often puts people, relationships and values into the weighing.
- J/P: the ENTJ side's J more often forms a structure outward and closes the arrangement into one version; the ENFP side's P more often keeps flexibility outward, holding options open for new information.

In the notation used here, ENFP is Ne–Fi–Te–Si and ENTJ is Te–Ni–Se–Fi. Both stacks include Fi and Te. Fi is auxiliary for ENFP and fourth for ENTJ, while Te is third for ENFP and dominant for ENTJ. The perceiving functions differ, and sources vary in how they label the third process.

These positions describe emphasis inside the model. They do not order behaviour, and they do not say who is better at firefighting or whether two people work well together. With the same delay notice on the table, either type may phone first, open the staffing sheet first, or go to the client first; the difference is not the first step but which kind of evidence gets cited, and under what conditions a close is acceptable.
sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
In a fictional project, both colleagues receive the same delay notice and can review the same alternatives. Either may contact the client or check staffing. What they do depends partly on their responsibilities and what the project needs.

The shared E concerns outward attention and energy. The shared N concerns giving weight to patterns and possibilities. The letters do not tell you which colleague will take the lead or how quickly the team will reach a decision.

The difference sits in the other two. T/F changes the basis: the ENTJ side more often asks which route loses less under the same constraints and whether that standard can be applied to every module; the ENFP side more often asks what this choice means for the client, the team and the person concerned, and whose situation has been left out. J/P changes how the close works: the ENTJ side more often closes dates, owners and the outward line into one version; the ENFP side more often keeps one more route open before settling, waiting for new information.

Both bases and both closings are available to both. When the client writes that any change of date means a claim, someone leaning ENFP may also converge quickly and drive execution; when the plan is clearly unworkable and the team has been working late for weeks, someone leaning ENTJ may also demand a different route.

### ENFP and ENTJ: the same delay notice, two kinds of basis

In a fictional project review, both colleagues receive the same delay notice, staffing information, sign-off requirements and supplier options. The opening date is unchanged.

For T/F, either colleague can assess the impact on the people preparing the launch or apply the same staffing, scope and deadline criteria to each option. For J/P, either can agree on a provisional plan or keep several workable options open while waiting for the same reply.

These are separate questions: what makes one option preferable, and when to commit to it. Either person can use both kinds of criteria and either approach to planning.

Each approach has a cost. Spread too wide, the team keeps changing direction and is back where it started two days later; close too fast, and what gets cut may be exactly what the client cares about most. The size of the cost has nothing to do with preference; it depends on who holds the supplier information, who has decision authority, and who signs for delivery.

The test has to leave room. Change the conditions and either may switch; a single choice describes this occasion's information and duty, and cannot be used to classify.

### ENFP and ENTJ: why Fi and Te are shared while both perceiving functions change

In the four-function notation used here, ENFP is Ne–Fi–Te–Si and ENTJ is Te–Ni–Se–Fi. What is shared is the two judging processes: Te third in ENFP and first in ENTJ, Fi second in ENFP and fourth in ENTJ. What changes is the perceiving pair: Ne to Ni, Si to Se.

The reason is that two letters change at once. J/P changes the category of the extraverted dominant process: both are E types in this model, and ENTJ's extraverted dominant is the judging process Te while ENFP's is the perceiving process Ne. That is a label of a theoretical category, not the order of real steps, and it does not mean that the one who judges first is more decisive. T/F changes the rank of the judging processes: both use standards and values, and what differs is which side gets leaned on first — Te ahead on the ENTJ side, Fi ahead on the ENFP side.

Both stacks include Fi and Te, but at different positions. The order describes the model and cannot establish who will make a better plan or work more effectively with clients.

Whether the third position (Te in ENFP, Se in ENTJ) is marked introverted or extraverted is not uniform across tables. This page takes the common version and treats it as a secondary clue only, not for inferring behaviour order or areas of strength. Base descriptions sit on the [ENFP profile](/en/personality/enfp) and the [ENTJ profile](/en/personality/entj).

sections.body_md:
Align the conditions first: the same number of delay days, the same people available, the same client, the same contract terms. If one is the project manager and the other only helping out, or the client has already written in a penalty, role and constraint will swamp both columns and the difference narrows.

Each row states which kind of evidence may be attended to first in the same scene, not a fixed action. Both types can take the other's approach; the table only describes what tends to be taken first, and the last column marks whether the row sits closer to T/F or J/P.

| The same scene (same delay, same people, same client) | ENFP: the kind of evidence likely to be taken first | ENTJ: the kind of evidence likely to be taken first | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What the first round of discussion adds | Weigh what the same delivery options mean for the people preparing the launch | Apply the same staffing, scope and deadline criteria to each delivery option | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F |
| Both assess the same options for three modules | Weigh how changes would affect customers and the teams that rely on each module | Apply the same capacity and acceptance criteria to every option | Decision criteria: T/F |
| How finished the plan is before it goes out | Keep several workable plans open while both wait for the same client feedback | Agree on a provisional plan and mark what may change after the same feedback | Outward stance, leaning J/P |
| Both decide what to prioritize in the same client update | Weigh what the change means for the people preparing to open the store | Apply the same criteria for relevance and accuracy used in comparable updates | Decision criteria: T/F |
| Both have the same assignments and staffing information still pending | Keep two workable staffing plans available until the same availability information is confirmed | Agree on a provisional staffing plan and set a time to review it | Approach to outward arrangements: J/P |
| Both plan a follow-up to the same review | Keep two feasible changes open until the team has the same feedback | Agree on one provisional change and set a time to revisit it | Approach to outward arrangements: J/P |

None of these rows is a scale of ability. An ENFP with years in delivery may open the staffing sheet first; an ENTJ just handed the project may ask everywhere for alternatives. Duty, experience, the amount of information and the deadline all rewrite the picture, and these rows only suggest where to look, never how to classify.
sections.title: ENFP and ENTJ in one minute

sections.body_md:
Boundary of use: the three scenes below are editorial demonstrations, used only to see how the same information gets read with different emphasis. They are not for typing and not for allocating posts. Whether a pairing works depends far more on who holds the supplier information, who has decision authority and who signs for the client.

### ENFP and ENTJ: covering a two-week delay the client will not accept

(Fictional scene) A store system was due to launch at month end; a third-party payment interface slipped and the whole thing moves to the middle of next month. The client replies with one line: the opening date cannot move, find a way.

One may go and ask first: can the payment provider open a sandbox, can another provider cover the interim, can the client open with checkout but without the membership feature. What is attended to is which routes remain and what each means for the opening. The other may lay the three routes out by cost first: switching provider means rebuilding the reconciliation, opening a sandbox needs the client to configure testing, cutting membership needs sales to agree; then fix one main route and one fallback, and write into the group when the decision must be made. Who takes which segment usually depends on who knows the provider and who can amend the contract, not on type.

The costs differ: too many routes and the team keeps turning, back at the start two days later; too fast a close and the part cut is the part the client cared about. A workable pairing agrees the exploration deadline and the give-ups in advance, with the deadline set by project complexity and contract milestones rather than a generic number of hours.

The evidence that counts is whether the plan states what is being given up. A plan listing only new actions and no give-ups usually breaks in the second week of execution. Counterexamples: with the client writing that any change of date means a claim, someone leaning ENFP may also converge immediately; when the team cannot sustain it, someone leaning ENTJ may also go to the client to renegotiate scope.

A check: write two versions of the recovery plan — one adjusting scope (what gets delivered less), one adjusting staffing (who joins, for how many days) — and mark in each the item that breaks first. If both point at the same place, check the shared bottleneck first: the same interface, the same approval, the same group of people. If they point at different places, align each assumption, dependency and acceptable loss, then see whether there really is a difference in risk appetite. Writing fast or slow cannot be used to judge preference.

### ENFP and ENTJ: mid-project, the technical approach turns out not to work

(Fictional scene) Four months in, the synchronous design drops orders when a store's network is unstable, and switching to asynchronous means rewriting half of it.

One may look first for a third route: local caching only in weak-network stores, pushing the drop rate down to something acceptable, a partial rollout across a few stores first. The other may calculate the cost of switching against not switching: how many person-weeks to rewrite half, whether the delay collides with a contract milestone, and what the worst-case compensation is if it does not switch.

Both calculations may conclude switch or do not switch, and may land on the same route for different reasons. Whether it is reversible has to rest on conditions: a small-scale trial only makes sense when dropped orders can be fully detected, reliably re-entered, and the affected scope is contained; if drops cannot be reconciled, key data cannot be recovered, or re-entry conflicts with reconciliation, the trial should not be widened until the risk is cleared. These conditions apply to both people equally and do not change with type.

### ENFP and ENTJ: a partner wants a twenty-thousand diving course

(Fictional scene) The way trade-offs are made at work turns up in a shared household too, with more constraints: budget, time, care arrangements, and what each person cares about.

In a fictional household decision, one partner wants to take a costly diving course that would occupy three weekends. Both can discuss what the experience would mean to the person taking the course and apply the same budget and scheduling criteria they use for similar commitments.

The household can consider personal value and practical constraints together. Either person can ask whether the budget can absorb the course, how responsibilities would be covered and why the course matters to their partner.

A check: each writes one line on when this money would count as well spent, then swaps and reads. If the two lines are far apart, align three things first: the budget ceiling, the care arrangement for those three weekends, and what each most wants out of it — the experience, the certificate, or doing it together. If both still want it after that, discuss whether to start with a trial session; instalments are a payment arrangement, not a conclusion, and whether it can be split depends on the provider and the household's cash flow.
sections.title: ENFP and ENTJ at work and in relationships

sections.body_md:
Reading ENFP as only producing ideas and never landing them is the most common misreading of this pair. In a recovery they often write the plan as a timetable too, only with more versions and faster revisions; more versions does not mean no landing, and fast revision does not mean no standard.

Reading ENTJ as indifferent to how the team feels is also wrong. Some ENTJs seek people out after the meeting, some do not; whether they care depends on the specific people and relationship, cannot be deduced from four letters, and cannot be deduced from one meeting where they did not respond.

The third misreads T/F as who is harder. In a recovery, hardness depends on the contract terms, the duty and the tolerable cost; the same person behaves completely differently in front of two contracts, one with a penalty clause and one without.

The fourth reads J/P as who is more urgent and who drags. J/P describes whether the outward stance leans closing or keeping open — not execution, and not reliability. Someone who closes fast may miss a condition; someone who keeps it open may be waiting for a reply that will never come.
sections.title: ENFP and ENTJ: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When two results differ, check the item bank, language version and scoring definition first, then the circumstances: were you signing for the outcome, did you have enough information, how tight was the deadline. People accountable for a result may be more likely to answer "cut the scope first"; circumstances push answers to one side, and a single score cannot establish a stable tendency.

Put the practice across several comparable situations rather than one reaction. Take three recent delays or last-minute changes and write three lines for each — which kind of information was added first, by what standard the trade-off was made, and whether the arrangement was closed into one version outward or left with options. If "what this means for the people involved" or "which standard applies consistently" keeps recurring, that is worth discussing as your habit of judgement; these are not typing rules and there is no threshold of how many cases makes a type.

items.answer:
Strictly, no. Either may phone first, open the staffing sheet first or go to the client first; the order depends more on role, duty, experience and deadline.

In the fictional delay, the effect on the people involved and the consistent criteria for comparing options illustrate T/F. Keeping alternatives open or agreeing on a provisional plan illustrates J/P. Either person can use both considerations and both approaches.
items.question: Facing the same bad news, can the first step tell them apart?

items.answer:
Because two letters change at once: T/F changes the rank of the judging processes, and J/P changes the category of the extraverted dominant process.

In the notation used here, ENFP is Ne–Fi–Te–Si and ENTJ is Te–Ni–Se–Fi. ENFP leads with Ne and uses Fi as its auxiliary. ENTJ leads with Te and uses Ni as its auxiliary. Both include Fi and Te in different positions, and sources vary in how they label the third process.
items.question: Why do they share Fi and Te while both perceiving functions change?

items.answer:
Yes, but not from a single action or from order.

What discriminates better is the reason and the conditions: under the same contract, who more often asks first what this means for the people involved, and who more often asks first which standard applies consistently and loses less; whether the arrangement is closed into one version outward or kept open for new information. Either type crosses over, especially when the client will not accept a delay or a penalty applies; crossing over shows the conditions changed, not the type.
items.question: An ENTJ also thinks up new routes, an ENFP also cuts scope — can they still be told apart?

items.answer:
Type cannot decide. Firefighting has four segments — mapping the gap, finding an alternative, settling a plan, accounting to the client — and which comes more easily depends on technical background, supplier relationships, decision authority and client constraints.

A workable split follows information and authority: whoever holds the technical and supplier information explores alternatives, whoever has decision authority and knows the client's constraints closes the plan. To practise discriminating, take a fictional delay notice and write two versions of the plan each, then compare which conditions, assumptions and give-ups each version missed, rather than which was written faster.
items.question: Which is better suited to firefighting or covering a gap?

items.answer:
Usually on when to stop discussing alternatives: one worries about closing too early, the other about never closing.

A workable agreement states three things in advance: the exploration deadline, who decides, and what evidence reopens the discussion — for example, the main route's key assumption being disproved. The deadline follows project complexity and contract milestones rather than a fixed duration; writing it into the group is more useful than arguing afterwards about who is more decisive.
items.question: Where do they most often jam when firefighting together?

items.answer:
Look first at whether the circumstances are changing, rather than deciding which type you are.

Check whether both results used the same questionnaire, language and scoring method. If the tool supplies comparable T/F and J/P scores and explains its thresholds, compare each pair separately. Context may shape which situations you recall when answering. Two results alone cannot establish what caused the difference.

The arrangement of the four positions on this page, in particular whether the third process (Te in ENFP, Se in ENTJ) is marked introverted or extraverted, follows the common writing as an editorial convention; other sources handle it differently, and this page does not present the writing as the Foundation's only reading, nor use position to predict behaviour order, areas of strength, collaboration outcomes or attraction.
